## TL;DR

Task #1185 fixes restart notices for RepoOS servers supervised by systemd or launchd. The reported systemd user service can have a process title renamed to `repoos-<project>`, while `systemctl status <pid>` identifies only the enclosing `user@<uid>.service` manager. This follow-up makes the detector inspect the process cgroup and parent in that inconclusive-success case, so it can recover the actual RepoOS unit and route restart through systemd. A regression test covers the specific status-success/cgroup-identifies-unit sequence.

## Work and rationale

The reported failure was not that systemd could not restart the service: a manual `systemctl --user restart` worked. The application had misclassified the server as hand-run because its process title no longer exposed the service name. The restart notice therefore offered a path that did not restart the supervisor-managed process.

The detector already parsed a usable service name from `systemctl status <pid>` and had cgroup and parent fallbacks for command failures. Review 6 exposed a gap in that branching: systemctl may exit successfully while describing the generic user manager, which the parser correctly rejects because restarting that unit would affect the entire user manager. The function then classified the result as uncertain before consulting the target process’s cgroup.

I extracted the cgroup and parent checks into a shared fallback and invoke it both when systemctl fails and when it succeeds without a parseable service unit. The existing cautious behavior remains: usable parsed units return directly; a fallback can identify a service or report an ambiguous systemd parent; otherwise the function preserves the prior uncertain/none decision based on systemctl output. The cgroup-derived restart command uses the user manager when the path is under `user.slice`.

The new test returns a successful status response naming `user@1000.service`, then provides a cgroup path containing `com.repoos.serve.tuk-driver-aaa442e5.service`. It asserts managed classification, the exact service name, the user-scoped restart command, and that the cgroup was read. The suite also retains detection coverage for cgroup-only discovery, parent fallback, external services, and a shell-parented hand-run server.

The earlier task work also routes restart actions for detected launchd/systemd units through their service managers and surfaces restart failures in the release notice. Existing UI progress/error fixture tests cover those states. The QA record states that no real hand-run server restart was performed in this session; automated tests are not presented as live server evidence.

## Approaches tried

I kept the parser’s rejection of `user@<uid>.service`: treating the user manager itself as the target would be unsafe and would not restart only the RepoOS server. Instead, I used process-specific evidence from `/proc/<pid>/cgroup`, which identifies the actual unit even when the command output is valid but too broad. Parent inspection remains the secondary fallback when cgroup data is unavailable. I added a test that exercises the successful-command branch directly, rather than relying only on tests where the systemctl mock throws; that makes the previously missing branch observable.

## Challenges and blockers

The subtlety was distinguishing command failure from successful but insufficient output. The former had already been covered, which made the missing behavior easy to overlook. The manual QA boundary also matters: this environment did not control the reported bee host or another real hand-run server, so the live restart acceptance check remains unverified. The QA note records that limitation explicitly.

## Key learnings

A supervisor query can succeed without identifying the process’s own service. Fallback detection should be triggered by inconclusive output as well as exceptions. Tests should model realistic command output and branching, not just parser inputs, especially when service-manager output includes an enclosing user or system scope. Finally, automated restart routing tests establish the intended command path but do not prove a live service restarted; that distinction should remain clear in release QA.
